title: Magnetic Particle Inspection of Castings and Forgings
description: MPI of castings and forgings to ASTM A275, E1444 and MSS SP-53, performed at your US plant, foundry or receiving dock. Request a quote with parts and specs.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection of Castings and Forgings Across the United States
html:
Magnetic particle inspection of castings and forgings finds surface and near-surface flaws such as cracks, laps, seams, hot tears and shrinkage that break the surface of steel valve bodies, flanges, fittings, shafts, gears and hooks. Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians to foundries, forge shops, machine shops, receiving docks and plants in the United States to examine to ASTM E1444, ASTM A275 and MSS SP-53 requirements and report every indication. To get started, request a castings and forgings MPI quote.

Why castings and forgings need their own technique

A weld is a thin, linear target; a casting or forging is a complex shape with thick sections, sudden changes in cross section, fillets, bores and parting lines. The flaws are different too. Castings can carry shrinkage cavities and hot tears where metal solidified unevenly, cold shuts where two streams failed to fuse, and surface porosity from gas. Forgings can carry laps and folds where metal was folded over during forming, seams inherited from the billet, quench cracks and grinding cracks introduced after heat treatment. Magnetic particle testing shows surface-opening versions of all of these on ferromagnetic carbon, low-alloy and martensitic stainless steel.

Because geometry strongly influences how a magnetic field travels, a procedure for one part rarely suits another. The technique is set by part shape, size and surface finish, not just by material.

Standards that apply

US purchase specifications, valve standards and construction codes reference a small group of documents for this work:

  • ASTM E1444 is the practice for magnetic particle testing, and it sits alongside ASTM E709, the guide used to write techniques. Both are common references in procedures for components.
  • ASTM A275 / ASME SA-275 is the magnetic particle examination method for steel forgings, with acceptance criteria tied to the purchase order or specification.
  • MSS SP-53 covers magnetic particle examination of steel castings and forgings used for valves, flanges, fittings and other piping components.
  • ASTM E125 provides reference photographs of magnetic particle indications on ferrous castings, which inspectors use to classify indications in specifications that cite it.
  • ASME Section V Article 7 covers technique requirements that a pressure-code user may call out; see our guide to Article 7 requirements.

Acceptance levels come from the purchase order, the valve or flange specification and the end-use code. We apply the one named in your documents and do not choose a level ourselves.

Bench units, portable yokes and part-specific magnetizing

Shop work on small and mid-size parts is usually done on a stationary wet horizontal bench, where the part is clamped between heads and current passes through it for circular magnetization while a coil adds longitudinal magnetization. Atlantis technicians often work at your site and so more commonly use portable equipment: yokes, portable coils and cable wraps. The right choice depends on size, weight and where the part sits.

  • Head shot. Current passes through the length of a part such as a shaft, creating a circular field that finds longitudinal cracks. Where we use portable contact equipment, arc burns are a risk, so contacts are padded and the procedure controls them.
  • Coil shot. A coil wrapped around or placed over the part creates a longitudinal field to find transverse cracks. Fill factor and part length affect the current that is needed.
  • Yoke. For flanges, valve bodies and large castings that cannot be placed on a bench, a yoke is moved across the surface in overlapping positions and two directions.
  • Residual versus continuous method. Continuous method, where particles are applied while the current flows, is the normal method; the residual method relies on the magnetism that remains and is limited to high-retentivity steels where the specification permits.

Receiving inspection and incoming material checks

Many orders for this work are receiving inspections. A purchaser takes delivery of valve castings, forged flanges or a batch of hooks and wants a sample or full examination before the parts are machined, assembled or welded into a system. Finding a cast or forging defect at the receiving dock is much cheaper than finding it after machining has added value. We can examine at your receiving area, plant floor or laydown yard, mark rejected pieces, and report each lot. Where specification allows sampling, the sampling plan comes from your purchase order, not from us.

Weld repairs of castings are a special case. A foundry may grind out a defect and weld the cavity; MT of the excavation before welding, and again after finishing, confirms the repair is sound. Weld-specific technique is covered on our magnetic particle weld inspection page.

Our penetrant testing and ultrasonic testing services cover the cases where MT is not the right tool, and the complete guide to magnetic particle testing explains the theory.

Surface preparation on cast and forged surfaces

As-cast surfaces are rough, scaled and sometimes sand-coated, and as-forged surfaces carry scale and tool marks. Rough surfaces trap particles and create non-relevant indications that look like cracks. The procedure states whether the surface must be blasted, ground or machined before examination and what finish is acceptable. Painted or primed parts need coating removed or limited to the thickness the procedure permits. We discuss surface condition before mobilization so the examination happens on parts that are ready.

Non-relevant indications on these parts are common: magnetic writing where parts touched, flux concentration at keyways and sharp section changes, and changes of permeability at weld repairs or heat-treated zones. A trained technician tells these from true flaws by re-magnetizing, re-cleaning and re-examining, and the report states what was done.

What the report contains

  • Part or lot identification, heat number, material specification and drawing or purchase order reference.
  • Procedure number and revision, the standard followed and the acceptance criteria named by the purchaser.
  • Equipment, magnetizing method, current values, particle type and lighting records, with calibration status.
  • Surface condition and temperature, and any preparation performed.
  • Technician and SNT-TC-1A level, with the Level III who approved the procedure.
  • Indications by location, orientation and length, sketched or photographed, and classified against the cited criteria or reference photographs.
  • Accept or reject status for each piece, as called out by the purchaser's criteria, with the final decision resting with the purchaser or the engineer.

Heat treatment, grinding and machining: when to examine

The point in the manufacturing route where MT is performed decides which flaws it can catch. Specifications for forgings usually require examination after heat treatment and rough machining, since quench cracks form during cooling and are most visible on a machined surface. Grinding cracks appear after final grinding of hardened parts such as gears and shafts, and a procedure that calls for a post-grind examination catches them before assembly. Castings are typically examined after cleaning and after any weld repair, and again after final machining on critical surfaces such as valve seats and sealing faces.

Purchasers who inspect only at receiving may miss flaws that machining later removes or exposes, so an examination plan that ties MT to named process points gives a clearer record. If you are unsure where the examination belongs, send us the route sheet and the specification, and we will propose hold points for your quality lead to approve. The final plan remains your decision, since it reflects your own customer's requirements.

Identification and traceability

Each examined piece should be traceable back to its heat or lot. We record the heat number, part number and serial marking where present, and we mark the part with an accepted method only if your specification allows. Low-stress stamping and etching are often restricted on pressure-retaining parts, so we use paint pens, tags or sketches where marking could harm the part. Rejected pieces are segregated by your staff according to your nonconformance procedure.

What to send for a quote

  • Part list with drawing numbers, sizes, quantities, heat numbers and material grades.
  • The governing specification, such as ASTM A275, MSS SP-53 or the purchase order, with the acceptance level and any E125 requirement.
  • Whether examination is at receiving, in process or on a finished part, and the required sampling.
  • Surface finish, coating and whether machining or blasting is complete.
  • Location, handling equipment, lighting and power, and site safety orientation or badging requirements.

Planning realities

Foundries and forge shops are hot, dusty and noisy, and parts may still be warm from heat treatment. Tell us the part temperature, since wet particles have temperature limits and dry powder tolerates more heat. Heavy parts need cranes or lift tables from your site, and fluorescent work requires a dark area that is often hard to find on a busy plant floor. We travel to your site with portable equipment; Atlantis has no office near it, so you should plan power, lighting and part staging as part of the scope.

Where we work in the United States

  • Detroit: automotive castings, forgings and drivetrain components.
  • Pittsburgh: steel forgings and heavy industrial castings.
  • Milwaukee: foundries and machinery component makers.
  • Birmingham: valve, pipe fitting and foundry products.
  • Houston: oilfield forgings, valve bodies and wellhead components.
  • Cleveland: forging and casting shops across northern Ohio.
  • Peoria: heavy equipment castings, shafts and gears.
  • Fort Wayne: forging, gear and drivetrain manufacturers.

See also industry pages for automotive, steel, oilfield, mining, rail and power, and the national magnetic particle testing page.

Training your own technicians

If a plant examines parts every day, in-house staff may be cheaper. Atlantis provides MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training aligned to SNT-TC-1A, with practice in the magnetic particle simulator. Under SNT-TC-1A the plant, not the course provider, issues the certification.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and it does not judge casting soundness for service beyond reporting indications against your criteria. Internal shrinkage and porosity deeper than the surface layer need other techniques, including ultrasonic testing where the part geometry allows. Our scope here stops at the three methods named on this page.

faq.q: What does MT find in castings that visual inspection misses?
faq.a: Tight surface cracks, hot tears, cold shuts and shallow subsurface flaws that are too fine or too dirty to see. The particles gather along the flaw and make it visible, even when the crack is only a few thousandths of an inch wide.

faq.q: Which standard governs magnetic particle examination of forgings?
faq.a: ASTM A275, adopted by ASME as SA-275, describes the examination of steel forgings. The purchase order or product specification sets acceptance levels, and ASTM E1444 and E709 support the technique.

faq.q: What is MSS SP-53 used for?
faq.a: MSS SP-53 describes magnetic particle examination of steel castings and forgings for valves, flanges, fittings and similar components. It is cited in valve and piping component specifications, which set the acceptance criteria.

faq.q: What are ASTM E125 reference photographs?
faq.a: E125 is a set of reference photographs showing typical magnetic particle indications on ferrous castings. Specifications that cite it let the examiner classify indications by comparing them with the photographs.

faq.q: Can you inspect austenitic stainless steel castings with MT?
faq.a: No, because austenitic stainless is not magnetic. Liquid penetrant testing is the normal surface method for those castings, and ultrasonic testing may be used for volume flaws where the grain structure allows.

faq.q: Do you inspect on a bench or on site?
faq.a: We usually work at your site with portable yokes, coils and cable wraps. If you have a stationary bench unit and need it operated, tell us when you request a quote so we can scope the work and write the procedure.

faq.q: What is the difference between head shot and coil shot?
faq.a: A head shot passes current through the part, giving a circular field that finds longitudinal cracks. A coil shot places the part in a coil, giving a longitudinal field that finds transverse cracks. Many parts need both.

faq.q: Can MT be performed on hot parts?
faq.a: Within limits. Wet particle suspensions have temperature ceilings and dry powder tolerates more heat, so the procedure states the allowed range. Tell us the part temperature and we will check it against the procedure before mobilizing.

faq.q: Who decides whether a casting is accepted?
faq.a: The purchaser, the specification or the engineer of record. We apply the acceptance criteria in your purchase order and report each indication with its location and size, so the decision maker has the facts.

faq.q: Do you do sampling inspection of incoming lots?
faq.a: Yes, if your purchase order or quality plan defines the sampling. We follow the plan you give us and report each part examined, including rejected pieces and the lot status your plan requires.
